title: A crisis protocol
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What is the first thing you do when a crisis hits?

Jose said that the class would work on a real situation a student brought, a crisis in a business, and he left the details of the dispute out of the class write-up. A student said: with any crisis it is important not to react emotionally, so take a step back and be methodical.
Jose said that the first reaction was emotional, anxiety and frustration that can turn into anger, so the first thing is: breathe. Then draw a mental map and write it down in bubbles.
He said that having it written down gives you ease, peace and reassurance, instead of the thought that you had better say this now or defend yourself.

Jose said that you pay attention to how the person omits or avoids information, because that shows bias. He said never start with a closed question or even a narrow one; start with an open question: please explain everything you know about the situation.
He said to act as if it were a trial and you were bringing in witnesses. A long explanation against a short one tells you something: detail means comfort, and no detail may mean omitting.

Jose said to mirror: imitate the communication style, tone, pace and volume. If you raise your voice, what happens? He gave a label: I see how frustrated you are, and I do not blame you for making that decision, it was a technical one.
He said: validate their feelings, not the facts. You are developing trust in the call by repeating back and paraphrasing, then pacing and leading: I agree with your approach, and then lead.

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write the last crisis you reacted to.
Write the breathing you will do first.
Write the mental map in bubbles.
Write the label and the validation.

check.q: What did Jose say to do first in a crisis?
What kind of question did Jose say to start with?
What did Jose say to validate?

recap: Breathe. Map it. Ask open. Mirror, label, validate.
